/blog/the-operations-audit-that-saves-tw.title: The operations audit that saves twenty hours a week — Scalar
/blog/the-operations-audit-that-saves-tw.description: Before you automate anything, map where the hours actually go. Most teams are surprised by which task turns out to be the expensive one.
h1: The operations audit that saves twenty hours a week
h2: Scale your growth, not your workload.
p: Before you automate anything, map where the hours actually go. Most teams are surprised by which task turns out to be the expensive one.

The instinct when a team feels overloaded is to automate the task that feels worst. Feeling is a poor guide. The task that generates the most complaints is often not the one consuming the most hours — it is simply the most irritating one.

A two-week audit, where everyone logs work in fifteen-minute blocks against a fixed category list, usually produces at least one genuine surprise. In our experience the expensive task is almost always a coordination task: chasing status, reconciling two systems that disagree, or rebuilding a report someone else already built.

Sort every logged hour into four buckets: work that creates value, work that moves information between systems, work that checks whether other work happened, and work that fixes errors. The second and third buckets are where automation pays immediately, and they are usually larger than anyone expects.
Once the audit is done the roadmap writes itself. You are no longer guessing which workflow deserves the first sprint — you have the hours in front of you.

/blog/from-spreadsheet-chaos-to-a-single.title: From spreadsheet chaos to a single source of truth — Scalar
/blog/from-spreadsheet-chaos-to-a-single.description: Every growing team hits the moment where the spreadsheet stops being a tool and starts being a liability. Here’s how to migrate without a freeze.
h1: From spreadsheet chaos to a single source of truth
h2: When the spreadsheet becomes the risk
Scale your growth, not your workload.
p: Every growing team hits the moment where the spreadsheet stops being a tool and starts being a liability. Here’s how to migrate without a freeze.

A spreadsheet is the correct tool for longer than most people admit. It is flexible, everyone can read it, and it costs nothing. The moment it stops being correct is specific and recognisable: when more than one person needs to write to it at the same time, and when a wrong cell has consequences nobody notices for a week.

At that point the spreadsheet is not a database with poor ergonomics. It is an unaudited system of record with no permissions, no history, and no validation, sitting underneath decisions that increasingly depend on it.

You do not need to stop work to move. Run the new system in parallel, write to both for two weeks, and reconcile daily. The reconciliation is the point — it surfaces every undocumented rule that lived in someone’s head, and there are always more of those than the team believes.
Only cut over once a full reconciliation cycle passes clean. Then make the spreadsheet read-only rather than deleting it; the archive costs nothing and settles arguments later.

/blog/what-to-automate-first-—-a-decisio.title: What to automate first — a decision framework — Scalar
/blog/what-to-automate-first-—-a-decisio.description: Frequency times fragility times hours. Three numbers that tell you which of your workflows deserves the first sprint — and which can wait.
h1: What to automate first — a decision framework
h2: Scale your growth, not your workload.
h3: Why fragility carries the most weight
p: Frequency times fragility times hours. Three numbers that tell you which of your workflows deserves the first sprint — and which can wait.
Deciding what to automate first is usually treated as a matter of judgement. It does not have to be. Score every candidate workflow on three axes and the ranking falls out on its own.

Frequency is how many times a week it runs. Fragility is how often it goes wrong or produces something that needs correcting, on a one-to-five scale. Hours is the time it consumes per run. Multiply the three. The workflow with the highest score is your first sprint, and it is very often not the one anybody nominated.

A task that runs constantly but never breaks is cheap to keep manual — people get fast at it. A task that runs less often but fails unpredictably is expensive twice over: once for the work, and again for the checking that the failure forces everyone else to do.
Rescore quarterly. Automating the top item changes the shape of everything below it, and the second sprint is rarely the workflow that ranked second the first time around.

/blog/designing-an-ai-agent-that-actuall.title: Designing an AI agent that actually ships work — Scalar
/blog/designing-an-ai-agent-that-actuall.description: An agent that drafts is a demo. An agent that files, routes and closes the loop is infrastructure. The difference is in how you scope the first version.
h1: Designing an AI agent that actually ships work
h2: Scale your growth, not your workload.
h3: Scope the first version around one closed loop
p: An agent that drafts is a demo. An agent that files, routes and closes the loop is infrastructure. The difference is in how you scope the first version.

The demo version of an AI agent writes a convincing first draft and hands it to a human. That is genuinely useful, and it is also where most implementations stop. The agent produces output; a person still does the filing, the routing, the follow-up, and the closing. The hours saved are real but modest.

The version that changes the economics is the one that completes the transaction. It writes the reply, sends it, logs it against the right record, sets the follow-up date, and escalates when the reply does not arrive. Each of those steps is unglamorous. Together they are the difference between a tool and a teammate.

Pick a single workflow with a clear beginning and a clear end, and automate all of it rather than most of several. A narrow agent that fully owns inbound lead qualification will outperform a broad one that half-owns six processes, because half-owned processes still require a human to hold the context.
Give it a hard boundary and an explicit escalation path. The agent should know precisely which cases it is not allowed to decide, and handing those off cleanly is a feature, not a limitation.

/blog/why-most-automation-projects-stall.title: Why most automation projects stall at the pilot stage — Scalar
/blog/why-most-automation-projects-stall.description: Nine in ten internal automation pilots never reach production. The blocker is almost never the technology — it’s that nobody owns the handover.
h1: Why most automation projects stall at the pilot stage
h2: The pilot is the easy part
Scale your growth, not your workload.
p: Nine in ten internal automation pilots never reach production. The blocker is almost never the technology — it’s that nobody owns the handover.

Almost every team we work with has already built something. A Zapier chain, a script a developer wrote on a Friday, a Notion database with three automations bolted on. It works. Someone demos it. Everyone agrees it should be rolled out. And then, six months later, it is still running on that one person’s account.

The failure is rarely technical. The pilot proves the workflow is possible; it does not prove the organisation can own it. Production means monitoring, error handling, a named owner, and a documented path for what happens when the API changes. Pilots skip all four, because skipping them is what makes a pilot fast.

Before a workflow leaves the pilot stage it needs three things written down: who is paged when it breaks, what the acceptable failure rate is, and which manual process it formally replaces. Without the third, the old process quietly survives alongside the new one and you have added work rather than removed it.

We build the handover document before we build the automation. It sounds bureaucratic for a two-week project, but it is the single strongest predictor of whether the thing is still running a year later.
